text:
[calm, conversational] Elon Musk says saving money is pointless.
Every month, you put a little money away.
For later. For the day you stop working.
In his future, you won't need it.
Machines will make almost everything, so cheaply that money won't matter anymore.
To him, saving is a bet against that future.
So what would have to be true for your savings to stop mattering?
He means it. The richest man on Earth has said it again and again this year.
But he has also told us how to check him.

Part of his future is already here: machines do more and more of the work.
But the part that would pay for your old age is still only a promise.
Last winter, on a podcast with the entrepreneur Peter Diamandis, he put it like this.

In other words: if his picture of the future comes true.
And behind that picture is a real argument, not a whim.
Artificial intelligence makes thinking almost free. Robots make labor almost free.
Then almost anything costs little more than its materials and the electricity to make it.
And when goods pile up faster than money, prices don't rise. They fall.
Everyone can afford what they want. He calls it universal high income.
Even he says he doesn't have it all figured out.

This isn't financial advice.
For his forecast to come true, four things have to happen. For his advice to be safe to follow, a fifth.
One: machines make almost everything.
Two: everything gets cheap.
Three: someone pays you an income.
Four: it arrives in time.
And five: if he's wrong, you're still fine.

[thoughtful] The first line is where he's closest to right.
Amazon's warehouses already run more than a million robots.
In offices, artificial intelligence writes first drafts, checks code, answers customers.
It isn't almost everything. Not yet. But it's spreading fast.
And by his own guess, superintelligence alone would give the world twenty to thirty percent more stuff.
That's a lot, he says. He's right.
But it isn't the end of money.
For that, he says, the economy has to reach into space: robots, rockets, and a launcher on the Moon.

So the first line: on its way.
But if machines make more and more, does everything get cheap?

Everything gets cheap.
This is the heart of his argument. And half of it is already true.
For every dollar a TV cost in the year two thousand, the same TV costs about two cents today.
Software and phone plans got cheaper too.
But for every dollar of hospital care back then, you now pay almost four.
Nursing homes, rent and college also rose far faster than prices overall.
The rule behind it is simple.
What a machine can copy gets cheap.
What takes a person's time, or a particular place, does not.
Now look at what you'll need most when you're old.

A home. A hospital bed. Someone to look after you.
Care costs what it does because it's a person's time. Their hands. Their patience. That's what makes it care.
A year in a nursing home already costs about as much as five years of the average Social Security check.
So the second line: half. Things got cheap. The things you need when you're old did not.
[warm] This channel exists for one reason: so that the arrival of superintelligence goes well for everybody. Including you, once you stop working. Want that too? Then subscribe.
[thoughtful] So when you stop working, who pays for your life?

Someone pays you an income.
His answer is a universal high income. This spring, he got more specific: checks from the federal government.
Remember his advice about retirement? It was an answer to a question. His host had just asked about the profits from all those machines.

Asked who would pay, he moved on to retirement advice.
To be fair, elsewhere in that conversation he named two ideas: prices will fall, and the government could just issue people money.
But today, there is no such income. No law. No amount. No budget.
In Congress, there are a few bills about artificial intelligence and jobs. None has passed.
And if the government just prints the money for those checks?
Homes, hospital beds, a nurse's hours: they don't multiply. That's where new money would push prices up.

The other way is the one his host asked about: tax the profits, and share them out.
This June, the Nobel-winning economist Daron Acemoglu asked whether that could be enough, if machines took over most jobs. His answer:

So the third line: only a promise. So far.
And even if it comes, will it come in time?

It arrives in time.
For a retirement, timing is everything.
Last winter, he said ten or twenty years. This summer, he named a year: twenty thirty-six.
Credit where it's due: that's a date you can check. But it's still a forecast. And your retirement won't wait for it.
By his own account, artificial intelligence moves much faster than government.
That's why he wants the simplest fix: just send people money.
But checks for everyone still need Congress. And the jobs could be gone long before Congress moves.
So how good are his dates?

One of his best-known is about cars.
In April twenty nineteen, on stage at Tesla's investor event about self-driving, he gave this date.

They came. Years late. A small fleet, not a million.
Earlier, on that same stage, he'd said it himself: sometimes he's not on time, but he gets it done.
That's fair. For a carmaker, late is fine.
For your retirement, late is the whole problem.
So the fourth line: if his record holds, years late.
What if he's not just late, but wrong?

If he's wrong, you're still fine.
This is the line his advice rests on.
Think of it as two bets.
You keep saving, and he's right: you put away money you never needed.
You stop saving, and he's wrong: you're old, and the money isn't there.
One mistake costs you a little. The other costs you your old age.
Nearly two in three Americans say they worry more about running out of money than about dying.
And the bet isn't the same for everyone.
Musk has said it's better to be an optimist and wrong than a pessimist and right.

He was talking about quality of life. There, he may have a point.
With money, it depends on who you are.
For someone who owns the machines, being an optimist and wrong costs almost nothing.
For someone with only a savings account, it can cost everything.
That's not a charge against him. It's simply where the risk lands.
So the fifth line: if he's wrong, the risk is yours.
Is there a way to make his promise safe to believe?

There is. It's been done before.
Musk himself expects the years ahead to bring radical change, social unrest, and immense prosperity.
People have lived through that once already.
When machines turned work upside down, they faced this same question: who takes care of us when we're old?
Germany answered first. In eighteen eighty-nine, an old-age pension became law, paid for by workers, employers and the state.
America followed in nineteen thirty-five. At the signing, President Franklin Roosevelt said why.

His answer wasn't a promise. It was a law.
With amounts, with dates, and with money set aside years before the first monthly check.
Then one winter, a retired woman in Vermont opened her mailbox. Ida May Fuller. Check number one.
She kept getting them until she was a hundred.
Not because someone was generous. Because the law said so.
Even this law needs repairs. Unless Congress acts, Social Security checks will shrink in the early twenty-thirties. Shrink, not stop.
That's the difference. A promise can be kept. A law has to be.

If machines really do take over the work, an income from all that abundance only counts once it's built the same way.
A right, written down, paid for before you need it.
The day you stop working: a check in your mailbox. Not because a forecast came true. Because a law says so.
That law doesn't exist yet. Writing it is up to voters and lawmakers.

The five lines, then.
One, on its way. One, half true.
And three that fail. The three that decide your old age: the income, the timing, and who carries the risk.
As advice, it fails its own test.

Maybe one day he'll be right. That future would be worth having.
But someone has to pay for the years in between.
Until a law does, that someone is you.
Saving was never a bet against the future. It's the bridge to it.
[warm] This channel exists for one reason: so that the arrival of superintelligence goes well for everybody, and everybody makes it across. Want that too? Then subscribe.
